component_var.text: `compute_loss_percentiles` takes a list of portfolio losses already sorted ascending and returns a dict of loss values at chosen quantile levels, which suits a fan chart showing how severe losses get across the distribution. `component_var` answers a different question: how much of a portfolio's total VaR comes from each position. It takes `weights`, `cov_matrix`, `portfolio_value` and an optional `confidence_level`, and allocates VaR to each asset via Euler allocation so the pieces sum to the total. In short, `compute_loss_percentiles` describes the shape of the loss distribution from loss data you supply, while `component_var` breaks one covariance-based VaR figure down by position.

explain.text: `compute_loss_percentiles` (Compute Loss Percentiles) takes a list of portfolio losses sorted ascending, where a loss is a positive number, and returns a dict of {percentile_label: loss_value} meant for fan chart display. For each requested quantile level `p`, it picks the loss at position `floor(p × n)` in the sorted list, capped at the last entry. You can pass your own levels between 0 and 1 via `percentiles`, or omit it to use the defaults: 0.50, 0.75, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99 and 0.995, which cover the standard regulatory range. The only required input is `sorted_losses`.

when.text:
`compute_loss_percentiles` (Compute Loss Percentiles) fits when you already have portfolio losses and want to see how the loss distribution looks across several tail levels.

- You have losses sorted ascending (losses as positive numbers) and want a percentile-to-loss dict for fan chart display.
- You want several tail levels in one call. By default it reports 0.50, 0.75, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99 and 0.995, or you can pass your own levels between 0 and 1 via `percentiles`.
- You want empirical quantiles read straight from the sorted losses, rather than from an assumed distribution.
- If you want parametric VaR bands across confidence levels and horizons instead, use `var_fan_chart`.
